title: Here are the primary rules for deciding the Ekadashi tithi in a pan...
body:
Here are the primary rules for deciding the Ekadashi tithi in a panchangam, along with the foundational verses found in the file Dharma Shastram.
Deciding the Ekadashi Tithi
The primary astronomical factor in determining the correct day for the Ekadashi fast is ensuring the tithi is completely free from the influence of the preceding lunar day, Dashami.
 * The Concept of Dashami Vedha (Overlap): According to the file Dharma Shastram, the determination of Ekadashi heavily relies on the absence of Vedha (overlap or intersection) with the Dashami tithi. The text specifically categorizes this Dashami Vedha into three distinct types: Arunodaya vedha, Suryodaya vedha, and Panchadashanadi vedha.
 * The Pre-Dawn Window (Arunodaya): The most critical time window to observe is Arunodaya, which is the pre-dawn period just before the sun rises. If the Dashami tithi is still active during this specific Arunodaya period, the corresponding Ekadashi is deemed Viddha (tainted).
 * Shuddha vs. Viddha Ekadashi: An Ekadashi is considered Shuddha (pure) only when the tithi is completely free from any trace of Dashami during the morning window. Fasting is traditionally prescribed on this Shuddha Ekadashi.
 * Smarta and Vaishnava Distinctions: The Dharma Shastram outlines different calculation nuances by providing dedicated sections for both Vaishnava rules (Vaishnava Ekadashi Nirnaya) and Smarta rules (Smarta Ekadashi Nirnaya). Vaishnava traditions, for instance, strictly reject an Ekadashi that has an Arunodaya Vedha, opting instead to observe the fast on the subsequent Dvadashi day.
 * Lost Tithis (Kshaya Tithi): In astronomical cases where the Ekadashi tithi is exceptionally short and is completely lost (lupta) between two sunrises, the observance of the fast is carried over to the Dvadashi tithi.
Adhara Shlokam (Foundational Verses)
The Dharma Shastram provides explicit Sanskrit verses governing these exact panchangam rules:
 * Prohibition of Dashami Overlap: To emphasize that an Ekadashi overlapping with Dashami at pre-dawn is unacceptable, the text quotes a specific verse. The verse states: "अरुणोदयकाले तु दशमी यदि दृश्यते । सा विद्धैकादशी तत्र पापमूलमुपोषणम् ॥". This dictates that if Dashami is visible during the Arunodaya period, that Ekadashi is considered tainted (Viddha), and fasting on such a day is the root of sin.
 * Rule for a Lost (Lupta) Ekadashi: When the Ekadashi tithi is skipped entirely, the observance shifts to the following day. The supporting verse for this scenario is: "एकादशी यदा लुप्ता परतो द्वादशी भवेत् । उपोष्या द्वादशी तत्र यदीच्छेत्परमां गतिम् ॥". This translates to: when Ekadashi is lost and Dvadashi follows, one should fast on that Dvadashi if they desire the highest spiritual goal.

title: Rules for Chaturthi in the Dharma Shastram
body:
Rules for Chaturthi in the Dharma Shastram
Based on the provided file, Dharma Shastram, the text outlines the foundational principles for determining the Chaturthi tithi, though it primarily details the general rule and the timing for Vinayaka Chaturthi rather than Sankashta Hara Chaturthi specifically.
 * The General Tithi Rule: The text establishes that Chaturthi is generally considered acceptable when it is Paraviddha (overlapping with the subsequent tithi, which is Panchami).
 * Adhara Shlokam (Foundational Verse): This is supported by a verse from Sage Vriddha Vasishtha which states: "एकादशी तथा षष्ठी अमावास्या चतुर्थिका । उपोष्याः परसंयुक्ताः पराः पूर्वेण संयुताः ॥".
 * Vinayaka Vratam Exception: For observances like Vinayaka Vratam, the text specifies that the tithi must be active during the midday period (Madhyahna Vyapini): "विनायकव्रतानुष्ठाने तु मध्याह्नव्यापिनी चतुर्थी ग्राह्या ।".
 * Supporting Verse: Sage Brihaspati corroborates this midday requirement: "चतुर्थीगणनाथस्य मातृविद्धा प्रशस्यते । मध्याह्नव्यापिनी चेत्स्यात्परतश्चेत्परेऽहनि ॥".
Determining Sankashta Hara Chaturthi
While the excerpted Dharma Shastram explicitly details the midday requirement for Vinayaka Vratam, Sankashta Hara Chaturthi operates on a different astronomical alignment because it is observed during the waning phase of the moon (Krishna Paksha).
 * The Moonrise Rule: Standard Dharma Shastras (such as the Nirnaya Sindhu) dictate that Sankashta Hara Chaturthi must be observed on the day when the Chaturthi tithi is active during Chandrodaya (moonrise).
 * Panchangam Calculation: When programming interactive calculators or scripts for lunar position tracking, the algorithm must first determine the exact local moonrise time for the user's specific geographical coordinates. If the Chaturthi tithi is prevailing at that exact moment of moonrise, that calendar day is finalized for the vratam.
 * Overlap Resolution: If Chaturthi spans the moonrise on two consecutive days, or if it is a short tithi that misses the moonrise entirely, traditional algorithms generally favor the day where the Chaturthi tithi intersects with the moonrise window most significantly.

body:
Because the core rule is strictly bound to the local sunset time, the exact date for Pradosham can vary based on geography. A panchangam calculated for India relies on Indian sunset times, which might result in a different observance date than one calculated for someone living in the United States.




Based on Dharma Shastram, there are specific adhara shlokas (foundational verses) under the "Nakta Vratam" (नक्तव्रतम्) section that explicitly define the Pradosha time and the rules for deciding the correct tithi.
Here are the primary statements and verses:
1. Defining the Pradosha Kala (Time Window)
The text defines Pradosha specifically in relation to sunset:
 * According to Sage Vyasa, the Pradosha period lasts for three muhurtas after the sun sets, and observances should be done during this time: "त्रिमुहूर्तः प्रदोषः स्याद्भानोरस्तंगते सति । नक्तं तत्र तु कर्तव्यमिति शास्त्रविनिश्चयः ॥".
 * Another Smriti verse corroborates this by stating Pradosha spans three ghatikas or three muhurtas post-sunset: "प्रदोषोऽस्तमयादूर्ध्वं घटिकात्रयमिष्यते । त्रिमुहूर्तः प्रदोषः स्याद्रवावस्तंगते सति ॥".
2. The Core Rule for Tithi Selection
The primary factor for accepting a tithi for Pradosham is its presence during the evening twilight window:
 * Sage Vatsa dictates that the tithi that overlaps with the Pradosha period is the one that must be selected (applicable to all tithis in both phases of the moon, except Ekadashi): "प्रदोषव्यापिनी ग्राह्या सदा नक्तव्रते तिथिः । एकादशीं विना सर्वा शुक्लकृष्णे तथा स्मृता ॥".
 * The Dharma Shastram establishes that pervasion of the tithi during the Pradosha period is the ultimate deciding factor: "तत्र प्रथमद्वितीययोः प्रदोषव्याप्तिर्निर्णायिका ।".
3. Resolving a Two-Day Overlap (Ubhaya Vyapti)
If the required tithi happens to be active during the Pradosha window on two consecutive days, the text provides a resolution:
 * The general rule states that if the tithi pervades the Pradosha time on both days, the latter day should be chosen: "उभयत्र तद्व्याप्तौ परतथिरेव ।".
 * This is supported by Sage Jabali, who states that when a tithi spans the Pradosha window on both days, the observance should take place on the subsequent day: "सदैव तिथ्योरुभयोः प्रदोषव्यापिनी तिथिः । तत्रोत्तरत्र नक्तं स्यादुभयत्रापि सा तिथिः ॥".

Deciding the correct date for Pradosham in a panchangam relies entirely on the relationship between the lunar day (tithi) and the local sunset time.
Understanding Pradosham and Trayodashi
Pradosham is an auspicious observance dedicated to Lord Shiva that occurs twice every Hindu lunar month. It always falls on the Trayodashi Tithi (the 13th lunar day) during both the waxing phase (Shukla Paksha) and the waning phase (Krishna Paksha) of the moon.
Defining the Pradosha Kala
The most critical factor in determining the exact date is the Pradosha Kala (the evening twilight window).
 * The Time Window: Pradosha Kala is the specific period surrounding sunset.
 * Duration: Traditionally, it is defined as lasting for 3 Muhurtas (approximately 2 hours and 24 minutes).
 * Sunset is Key: In practical application, this window typically begins about 1.5 hours before the local sunset and concludes about 1 hour after sunset.
Panchangam Rules for Deciding the Date
Because Hindu lunar tithis vary in length and do not align perfectly with standard 24-hour days, panchangam makers use the following standard rules to finalize the date:
 * The Primary Rule: Pradosha Vratam must be observed on the day when the Trayodashi Tithi is active during the Pradosha Kala (the sunset window).
 * Single-Day Overlap: If Trayodashi is active during the sunset period on only one specific day, that day is definitively chosen for the observance.
 * Two-Day Overlap: If Trayodashi starts before sunset on the first day and is still active during sunset on the second day, the panchangam generally selects the day where the tithi prevails for the maximum portion of the Pradosha Kala. Often, the first day is favored if the tithi is well-established before sunset.
 * No Overlap (Rare): If the Trayodashi tithi is exceptionally short and entirely misses the sunset window on both days, traditional Dharma Shastras typically recommend observing the vratam on the day the tithi begins.

title: Budha Maudhyam (Mercury Combustion) Surya Siddhanta 14° Limit
body: Surya Siddhanta VII.13-14 strictly sets 14° for direct Mercury and 12° for retrograde Mercury. Atichara motion uses 12° threshold in reference panchangams.

title: తిథి సమయాలు ప్రత్యక్షంగా దృగ్గోచరం కావు (12° కోణాంతర గణితం)
body: తిథి ఆకాశంలో కనిపించే గీత కాదు. సూర్య-చంద్రుల స్ఫుట దీర్ఘాంశ భేదం ప్రతి 12° మారినప్పుడు తిథి పూర్తవుతుంది. టర్మినేటర్ వేగం ~15.4 km/h అయినప్పటికీ కంటితో చూసి తిథి ముగింపును నిర్ణయించడం అసాధ్యం. సూర్య సిద్ధాంత, దృగ్గణిత సూక్ష్మ గణితం చేతనే నిర్ణయించాలి.

title: గ్రిగోరియన్ ఆధారిత పౌర క్యాలెండర్ vs వైదిక నిరయణ సిద్ధాంతం
body: గ్రిగోరియన్ క్యాలెండర్ లౌకిక అవసరాలకు సాయన విషువత్ కాలం స్థిరంగా ఉంచేందుకు ఏర్పడింది (లీప్ డే). వైదిక ధర్మాచరణకు సనాతన సూర్యసిద్ధాంత శుద్ధ నిరయణ గణితమే ప్రమాణం. క్షయ-అధిక మాసాలు వైదిక నిరయణ చాంద్రమానంలోనే సంభవిస్తాయి.
